text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
- Mild weather in February doesn't bring any relief to unemployment situation. 4.67 million without job in February, gain of 13,600.
- FDP demands pension increases for those who raise children. More burdens for people without children.

- Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber in row over Stoiber's suggestion for motorway-user fee. Waigel calls it "adventuresome" and rejects idea of allocating revenues from such a fee to motorway construction.
- Economy only moving slowly forward. Companies more sceptical as the government. Investors holding back, according to DIHT spring survey of companies.
- Government coal subsidies should be cut to 3.8 billion marks from 10 billion marks by year 2005.
- Unemployment reaches new record level. Further job cuts especially in eastern Germany. DIHT expects the low point to come in the autumn.
- No agreement reached after coal talks between union leaders and Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
- Rising costs plague chemical industry. Employers demand cuts in supplementary wage costs. While workers accepting modest pay raises, supplementary wage costs keep rising, chemical companies say.
- Unemployment rises to new postwar record with 4.7 million people without job in February.

- Bundestag president Rita Suessmuth says women should not be put at disadvantage with pension rights. She says she opposed to proposal from Christian Democrats to cut pension levels in 2010 rather than in 2030 because it would hit women harder.
- Lower Saxony says it remains opposed to further nuclear waste transports. But state interior minister Gerhard Glogowski admits state has no means to block transports.
- Companies eliminate more jobs in February.
- Doubts rise about any agreement on taxes. Coalition accuses SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine of lacking willingness to compromise.
